Q: Display negative values in brackets A:

For SQL Server 2012 and higher, an alternative is to use the FORMAT function to enclose a negative number in parentheses.

A small limitation is that you will need to specify a maximum number of decimal places.

WITH T AS
(
    SELECT -1361236.75886298 AS N UNION ALL
    SELECT -2000 UNION ALL
    SELECT 2000 
)    
SELECT 
     FORMAT ( N, '#,###.##########;(#,###.##########)') 
FROM T

Results:

(1,361,236.75886298)
(2,000)
2,000

Q: Is it possible to have vars in a slurm preamble? A:

No that is not possible as per the documentation

Or do I need to move that stuff to the command line when I submit

That would be a solution in many cases, but the name of the compute node will not be known at that time so it will not work here

or dynamically create the slurm file?

Yes that should be the option, redirect the main command to that file

./my_program ... > logs/job_notebook_${NODE_NUM}.out

or redirect the whole output by inserting the following, as first lines after #SBATCH directives

NODE_NUM=$(echo -n $HOSTNAME | tail -c 1)
exec > logs/job_notebook_${NODE_NUM}.out

Q: User Interface Using Tkinter to display a Chessboard A: 
import tkinter as tk
import chess

class ChessGame:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = root
        self.root.title("Simple Chess")
        self.board = chess.Board()
        self.selected_square = None
        
        # UI Setup
        self.canvas = tk.Canvas(self.root, width=400, height=400)
        self.canvas.pack()
        self.canvas.bind("<Button-1>", self.handle_click)
        
        self.draw_board()

    def draw_board(self):
        self.canvas.delete("all")
        colors = ["#eeeed2", "#769656"] # Light and Dark squares
        
        for r in range(8):
            for c in range(8):
                color = colors[(r + c) % 2]
                x1, y1 = c * 50, r * 50
                x2, y2 = x1 + 50, y1 + 50
                self.canvas.create_rectangle(x1, y1, x2, y2, fill=color, outline="")
                
                # Draw Pieces
                square = chess.square(c, 7 - r)
                piece = self.board.piece_at(square)
                if piece:
                    self.canvas.create_text(x1 + 25, y1 + 25, 
                                           text=self.get_unicode_piece(piece), 
                                           font=("Arial", 32))

    def get_unicode_piece(self, piece):
        # Maps chess pieces to Unicode symbols
        symbols = {
            'R': '♖', 'N': '♘', 'B': '♗', 'Q': '♕', 'K': '♔', 'P': '♙',
            'r': '♜', 'n': '♞', 'b': '♝', 'q': '♛', 'k': '♚', 'p': '♟'
        }
        return symbols.get(piece.symbol())

    def handle_click(self, event):
        col = event.x // 50
        row = 7 - (event.y // 50)
        square = chess.square(col, row)

        if self.selected_square is None:
            if self.board.piece_at(square):
                self.selected_square = square
        else:
            move = chess.Move(self.selected_square, square)
            if move in self.board.legal_moves:
                self.board.push(move)
            elif chess.Move(self.selected_square, square, promotion=chess.QUEEN) in self.board.legal_moves:
                # Basic auto-promotion to Queen
                self.board.push(chess.Move(self.selected_square, square, promotion=chess.QUEEN))
            
            self.selected_square = None
            
        self.draw_board()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    root = tk.Tk()
    game = ChessGame(root)
    root.mainloop()

Q: How Do You Test a Bitfield in Assembly? A:

I'll focus on code size as the metric, since you haven't identified a specific CPU for which we could count clock cycles, and presumably the time spent on this instruction sequence is swamped by that of the preceding BIOS call.

It was noted that the bits of interest are all in the low byte, so we can do this with 8-bit instructions, which can be shorter. Since we're doing everything within AX, we have the "accumulator-immediate" ALU instructions; these are 2 bytes for an 8-bit instruction (opcode plus 1-byte immediate), and 3 bytes for a 16-bit instruction (opcode plus 2-byte immediate).

Your solution then is

mov ax, [addr]                    ; 3 bytes
and ax, 0b0000000010011001        ; 3
cmp ax, 0b0000000010011001        ; 3
jne missing_bits                  ; 2

for a total of 11 bytes.

So we can get down to 9 by doing shorter than your solution to do

mov al, [addr]     ; 3 bytes
and al, 0b10011001 ; 2
cmp al, 0b10011001 ; 2
jne missing_bits   ; 2

Several of the 16-bit options below can be adapted into solutions of the same length, but I didn't find anything shorter.

If the bits of interest span both bytes of the word, then what compilers do is the equivalent of

mov ax, [addr]    ; 3 bytes
not ax            ; 2
test ax, mask     ; 3
jnz missing_bits  ; 2

so that "all these bits should be 1" is transformed into "all these bits should be 0". Then after masking off the other bits, we are checking for the entire register to be zero, which is given to us by the zero flag.

We can get one byte shorter by doing

mov ax, [addr]      ; 3 bytes
or ax, ~mask        ; 3
inc ax              ; 1
jnz missing_bits    ; 2

By ORing with the complement of the mask, all the desired bits were set if and only if the result is all-bits-1, or -1 in two's complement; then adding 1 results in 0.

This takes advantage of the single-byte inc encoding, but note that it's 16-bit only (or 32-bit in 32-bit mode); using inc al in the 8-bit solution would be 2 bytes. Also, these encodings were removed entirely in 64-bit mode (they were reused for the REX prefixes).

As far as speed is concerned, Peter Cordes noted that some older machines can only fuse test / jcc or cmp / jcc into a single uop, while newer CPUs (Sandybridge-family and Zen 3 and later) can also fuse inc / jcc.
